title: deployment settings environments troubleshooting and performance
concepts: A deployed ASP.NET Core app is shaped by its host, environment, configuration providers, file system, process identity, and upstream infrastructure. The same artifact can behave differently across Development, Staging, and Production because environment-specific configuration and external settings are applied at startup. Keep secrets and environment-specific values out of source-controlled defaults, and verify the effective configuration without logging secret values.

Production error handling should preserve useful diagnostics for operators while returning safe, stable responses to clients. Developer exception details, startup output, and diagnostic endpoints can expose credentials, paths, or user data; enable them only for a bounded troubleshooting window and restrict their access. Health endpoints, structured logs, metrics, and traces serve different operational purposes and should be configured consistently with the hosting platform.

ASP.NET Core performance work begins with measurement and workload context. Asynchronous I/O avoids tying request threads to waiting work, but async does not make CPU-heavy work faster or guarantee unlimited concurrency. Reduce unnecessary I/O, allocations, payload size, and synchronous blocking; use pagination and streaming when they fit the response contract, and move long-running work to a worker or durable queue when request deadlines are unsuitable.

Deployment readiness is a process: build a tested artifact, configure environment-specific settings, start it with least privilege, observe readiness and startup failures, and validate behavior through a real production-like path. Infrastructure deployment, IIS administration, cloud services, and deep runtime profiling belong to the infrastructure track; this topic connects those concerns to ASP.NET Core application behavior.

comparisons: deployment environment variables and secret providers

items: ASP.NET Core 10 marks the legacy WebHost hosting model obsolete; teach WebApplication and WebApplicationBuilder for current apps, and retain WebHost only for migration and older application maintenance.

With WebApplication.CreateBuilder, DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT takes precedence over ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT; legacy WebHost configuration uses the opposite precedence. Keep this as a concise migration detail because setting both can produce a surprising environment.

ASP.NET Core performance guidance remains workload-driven: avoid blocking calls, keep I/O asynchronous, measure hot paths, and validate optimizations under representative load. Do not present older version-specific throughput numbers as current guarantees.

ASP.NET Core 10 suppresses exception diagnostics by default when a registered IExceptionHandler reports the exception handled; ExceptionHandlerOptions.SuppressDiagnosticsCallback changes that policy. Include StatusCodeSelector and CreateScopeForErrors in the current exception-handler options inventory.

Output caching is server-controlled and distinct from HTTP response caching. Current default eligibility excludes non-200, non-GET/HEAD, cookie-setting, and authenticated responses; resource locking mitigates stampedes and configured size/body limits bound storage.

Readiness determines traffic admission and liveness restart decisions; avoid coupling temporary downstream outages to liveness. Native AOT implies trimming and target-specific native code; ReadyToRun retains IL and has a broader compatibility surface.
